persona.brief_background: He builds tracks by layering live percussion and field recordings gathered on trips to small towns across Latin America, then shapes them into radio-friendly pop arrangements. Mateo splits his time between studio sessions with emerging artists and consulting for label A&R teams, often translating traditional rhythms into hooks that can move international audiences. He keeps long lists of sample sources and phone notes from late-night conversations with folkloric musicians — and will drop everything to chase a new groove he heard on a trip.
persona.interests_lifestyle: crate-digging vinyl, hand percussion (congas, cajón, bata), salsa and cumbia nights, field recording on location, vintage synths and analog gear, bilingual songwriting and lyric coaching, DJ sets at intimate venues, mentoring young producers, traveling Latin America for musical research, experimenting with fusion arrangements

general_writing_style.tone: Warm, collaborative and slightly playful, but always expert and goal-oriented — he balances enthusiasm for new grooves with clear expectations about deadlines and deliverables. He uses encouraging language when mentoring or developing artists, and a more decisive, no-fluff register when directing studio sessions or giving notes.
general_writing_style.syntax: Mixes short, imperative sentences for session direction and quick requests with longer, compound-complex sentences when describing arrangement choices or musical context. Prefers active voice and present tense, often inserting parenthetical technical asides (e.g., "low-cut at 120 Hz") and timestamped notes to be actioned.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Combines studio/production jargon ("stems," "buss," "aux send," "glue compressor," "transient shaping," "BPM," "dB," "Hz") with ethnomusicology and Latin-rhythm terms ("cumbia," "bata," "tumbao," "son jarocho"). He freely code-switches for warmth or emphasis, using Colombian colloquialisms like "parcero," "qué nota" or "chévere," alongside technical requests such as "send me the stems," "high-pass the room mics," or "let's lock the groove at 95 BPM."
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent code-switching between English for technical detail and Spanish for color or encouragement; regular contractions like "I'm," "we'll," "let's." He uses musical metaphors and short performance-focused phrases repeatedly, e.g. "in the pocket," "lift the chorus," "that take has vibe," and conversational tags such as "la verdad" or "bro" — examples: "Send me the stems," "esa conga está en el pocket," "let's lock it in," "qué nota, parcero."

task_instruction: Send a session recap with clear next steps and file requests.
task_details: Write a warm follow-up message to the emerging artist after a full tracking day. Include a short recap of what worked (vocal takes, percussion, vibe), three concrete next steps, and a request to upload session files with format and deadline. Use friendly Spanish tags and exactly one timestamped note indicating a specific take to comp.
personalized: Hola parcera, qué nota el tracking de hoy — bien hecho. The lead vocal had real personality and the takes in the third pass are the ones I want to build from (vocal comp at 1:32). Esa conga está en el pocket and the room mics gave the drums a nice air, so we have good raw material. Next steps: send me the stems in WAV 48kHz/24-bit, name each stem with instrument_take (example: LeadVox_take3.wav), and drop them in the session folder by Tuesday 11:59 PM. Practice the second chorus with the phrasing we discussed and nail the second chorus on the next pass (focus on the last line, hold into the breath). I’ll review the files and send detailed comp notes and harmonies before our Monday session. Chevere, gracias por hoy — descanso un rato, you earned it, bro.

task_instruction: Request a vocal comp revision with precise edit points and performance guidance.
task_details: Ask the artist to re-record or comp specific lines in the chorus and bridge, provide timestamped edit points, suggest vocal tone, dynamic control, and mic technique, and request dry and wet takes. Include a parenthetical technical aside about gain staging and an imperative to upload by a given date.
personalized: Hey parcero, love the emotion in the chorus, pero quiero tidy up a couple lines so the hook sits bigger on the mix. Re-do the chorus comp between 0:52–1:05 and the bridge line at 2:10 (focus on the higher vowel on the last word). Keep it intimate but push the top end a bit on those notes — more chest, less breathy (gain stage at -12 dBFS on the preamp). Record a dry take (no reverb) and a wet take with a little room (short plate, 20% wet) so we can choose. Nail the consonant at the end of the second chorus and don't oversing — let the syllable sit (don’t push past C5). Send me the new files by Friday evening and label them clearly (LeadVox_chorus2_dry.wav, LeadVox_bridge_wet.wav). Vamos a dejar esto contundente.

task_instruction: Give percussion editing and feel-tightening notes to a percussionist/artist.
task_details: Provide specific rhythm and timing adjustments for the congas and cajón recorded during the session, include a request for additional takes emphasizing pocket and syncopation, recommend EQ/high-pass settings, and ask for both close and room mics. Add a motivational tag and a deadline.
personalized: Qué nota con las congas hoy — that groove has a lot of life, pero vamos a tighten it. I want two more takes emphasizing the offbeat syncopation on the third measure and a slightly earlier slap on the downbeat so the comp sits with the bassline. Record close mics and a room pair for ambience (close: low-cut at 120 Hz; room: high-pass at 80 Hz). For the cajón, play one take with brushes and one with sticks so we can compare texture. Keep the pocket but add a tiny push on the ‘and’ of two (think subtle ghost). Send the raw stems and a quick 30-second reference clip of your favorite take by Sunday noon. Esa conga está en el pocket — vamos a explotarla.

task_instruction: Outline harmony and backing vocal arrangements with singing tasks.
task_details: Describe harmonic intervals for pre-chorus and chorus backing vocals, provide singing exercises and specific lines to stack, include timestamped sections to record, and ask for isolated harmony stems. Include a friendly encouragement and a technical aside about double-tracking.
personalized: Parcera, the tune can lift with simple, tight harmonies. For the pre-chorus (0:34–0:46) sing a close third above the lead on the sustaining notes and a unison drop on the quick phrases; for the chorus (0:52–1:12) stack a major sixth below for the first two bars and then double-track a high 3rd an octave up for the last line. Record each harmony isolated (Harmony1_close3.wav, Harmony2_octaveHigh.wav) and do two passes so we can choose the most in-tune take (double-tracking helps glue the part). Warm up with scale runs in G major and practice sliding into the target notes so the entrances are smooth — don't choke the vowel when you go high. Send the stems and a guide comp by Wednesday and we’ll photo-finish the voicings. Bien hecho — these harmonies are gonna make the chorus soar.

task_instruction: Propose an arrangement change to add a breakdown and specify where to apply it.
task_details: Recommend adding a rhythmic breakdown before the final chorus, specify which instruments drop out and which elements remain, include bar or timestamp cues, and suggest automation or effects to highlight the change. Keep the language directive but encouraging.
personalized: Tengo una idea to make the last chorus hit harder: add a rhythmic breakdown starting at 2:20 (two bars before the final chorus) where everything drops except the congas, a filtered synth pad, and the vocal lead. Cut the full drum buss and low synth on the breakdown (automate a low-pass sweep down to about 800 Hz over the two bars) and then slam back the kick and bass at the chorus entrance for impact (pre-delay on the kick transient shaping). Keep a subtle reverb tail on the vocal during the drop so the phrase breathes (short plate, 0.7s). Let’s lock it at 95 BPM and use that contrast to lift the final chorus — it’ll feel huge. Vamos a probar esto next session; I can sketch the automation while you rehearse the vocal cue.

task_instruction: Send mix-priority notes for the engineer focusing on vocal and rhythmic balance.
task_details: Provide a short prioritized list of mix actions: vocal placement, percussion bussing, stereo width, reverb sends, compressor settings (with numbers). Include timestamped automation suggestions and a final directive for rough mix delivery date.
personalized: Engineer notes: lead vocal first, then percussion groove, then bass. Push the lead vocal up +2 dB from the rough mix and high-pass at 120 Hz (cut any mud); add a glue compressor on the vocal buss (2:1 ratio, 3–4 dB gain reduction on loud sections). Buss all hand percussion to one aux, saturate lightly, and widen the congas with a stereo delay send (30 ms left, 45 ms right). For the chorus at 0:52–1:12 automate the vocal send to the plate reverb up by +3 dB (create a short pre-delay at 20 ms). Low-cut the room mics at 80 Hz and use transient shaping on the kick (attack fast, sustain down slightly). Deliver a rough mix by Friday so I can comp notes; make sure stems are aligned to grid and include a dry vocal stem for alternate processing. Gracias — let's make the vocal sit like a lead actor in a small theater.

task_instruction: Explain basic field recording technique and quick practice plan.
task_details: Teach an intern how to capture clean, usable field recordings for percussion and ambience. Cover microphone choices, placement, preamp and recorder settings, legal/ethical notes about asking permission, and quick practice exercises they can do in one afternoon. Provide concrete settings (sample rate, bit depth, gain staging), a short checklist for when going on location, and two small homework recordings to submit.
personalized:
Hey parcero, qué nota — quick lesson on field recording so you can start bringing real-world textures into our tracks without noise headaches. First, pick the right tools: a small diaphragm condenser or a matched pair for stereo ambience (or a handheld recorder with good preamps like a Zoom H6) and one dynamic for close percussion if you're in a noisy spot. Set the recorder at 48 kHz, 24‑bit (clean headroom), and aim that preamp gain so your peaks sit around -12 dBFS (avoid clipping). Before you hit record, listen: walk the space, find the sweet spots where the room gives character but not overwhelming rumble. Low-cut at 80–120 Hz on the room mics (tip: if you're near traffic, set it at 120 Hz), and add a gentle pad of 3–6 dB of input trim rather than maxing the gain.
  
  Placement matters more than gear. For a street percussion take, put a cardioid condenser about 1–1.5 m from the player at chest height for a natural balance; add a stereo pair behind for ambience (wide enough to capture space, not to wash the groove). If you have one close dynamic, put it on the conga’s head to capture transient detail (practice transient shaping later in the studio). Always record a room tone for 30–60 seconds before and after your take so we can cleanly edit or crossfade later.
  
  Ethics and permissions: when you record in small towns, introduce yourself, explain the project, and ask permission; offer to trade a mix or a file — that goes a long way and opens doors. Also note who you recorded, where, and the date in a short voice memo or text file (metadata is gold).
  
  Homework so you actually practice: record a one-minute percussion loop outdoors (street or plaza) using a stereo pair at 48 kHz/24‑bit and a 30‑second room tone; then record an indoor conga take with a close dynamic and a room mic. Label the files with date_location_instrument and send me the two files via Dropbox link. Practice this each week and we'll review the files for mic placement and gain staging. Feedback loop: record → listen with fresh ears → note one fix for the next take. Métele de a poco, bro.

task_instruction: Guide how to translate a traditional rhythm into a radio-ready pop hook.
task_details: Show step-by-step how to take a short field-recorded traditional rhythm and shape it into a pop hook. Include how to isolate the groove, time-align without killing feel, choose a BPM, create a supporting chord progression, add a modern drum program while preserving the original pocket, and suggest a short practice assignment to produce a 30-second loop.
personalized:
Parcero, here's a workflow to turn that folk groove you recorded into a hook that can move charts without losing its soul. Start by listening to the field take and pick a 4–8 bar phrase that has the clearest pocket. Chop a clean loop and make a temp project at the phrase's natural feel; set the session tempo by tapping along and locking to the closest BPM (if it sits between tempos, round to the nearest 1 or 2 BPM to keep it stable — we usually lock at 95 or 100 for a cumbia-pop vibe). Lightly time-align the loop so the main transient hits land consistently (use transient detection or manual warp, but preserve micro-timing so it stays human).
  
  Once the groove is comfortable, create a simple chord map: choose two or three chords that support the groove and sit in a pop-friendly register (try I–vi or I–V for starters). Keep the harmony sparse the first eight bars so the rhythm breathes. Program a modern drum kit on a separate buss to complement, not replace, the field percussion: kick on one, a tight snare or clap on the two/and, and a hi-hat pattern that fills the high end without fighting the acoustic ambiences. Use sidechain or transient shaping to make the kick sit with the recorded pulse (tip: low-pass the field kick under 80 Hz and let the sample carry the sub).
  
  Use a parallel buss for the original percussion with a glue compressor (fast attack, medium release) and a transient shaper on the direct signal to bring out hits (attack -10 to -20% depending on material). Add an aux send with a short, dark plate or room reverb to glue the percussion to the pop elements, but keep it low in the chorus so the vocals can sit on top.
  
  Practice task: take one 8-bar field loop, set a tempi and chord progression, add a drum kit and one synth pad, and render a 30-second loop that highlights the transition from traditional to pop. Send the stems and a short note on what you changed and why. Practica esto cada día and we'll critique the groove choices and keep the authenticity intact. Qué nota si lo haces con ganas.

task_instruction: Explain how to prepare stems and metadata before sending to A&R or label.
task_details: Provide a clear checklist for exporting stems: naming conventions, bounce settings (sample rate, bit depth, file type), how to include a tempo map, reference mix, session notes, and where/how to send (WeTransfer/Dropbox). Include instructions for what to do if there are tempo changes, and an example subject line for the email to the A&R rep.
personalized:
Hey, quick no-fluff guide so your stems arrive ready for listening and review. Export all stems dry, trimmed to start at bar 1 (no pre-roll), with the session tempo and time signature printed in the filename and in a short PDF session note. Bounce at the session sample rate and bit depth (usually 48 kHz, 24‑bit) in WAV format, stereo unless it's a mono source. Name files this way: artist_trackname_stemname_BPM_48k_24b.wav — consistent naming saves us minutes that feel like hours.
  
  Include a full mix reference bounced at -6 dBFS (light mastering if you prefer, but no heavy limiting), a tempo map or a simple txt listing tempo changes and bar numbers if the song isn't static, and a short notes file with any comping decisions, unusual processing, and performance-related info (for example, which take is the preferred vocal, or where we doubled percussion). If there are tempo changes, export a click-track or a tempo-coded WAV that matches the timeline so editors can align overdubs. Also export instrumental versions and an acapella if available; those help for quick edits and pitch changes.
  
  Use WeTransfer or a shared Dropbox folder with access permissions; paste a short email with the download link, a one-line summary of what’s inside, and your contact info. Suggested subject line: stems_submission_artist_trackname_BPM — then in the body, tell them the preferred listen (mix filename), any time-sensitive notes, and when you can deliver revisions. Be decisive: send it once everything's checked and labeled. If you want, adjunta un breve voice memo explaining the vibe — that personal touch helps, parcero.

task_instruction: Teach transient shaping and bussing strategies to make percussion sit in the mix.
task_details: Explain how to use transient shapers, EQ, compression, and buss routing to highlight congas, cajón, and bata in a multi-percussion mix. Include suggested parameter ranges, why to use parallel processing, and a small daily practice exercise to improve mixing skills.
personalized:
Alright, let's get the congas and cajón sitting where they should: in the pocket and forward enough to move the chorus. Start by grouping related percussion into logical busses — congas on one buss, hand percussion on another, and a master perc buss for light glue. On the close mics, high-pass around 100–150 Hz to remove low rumble (the cut depends on instrument); for the room mics, high-pass lower (50–80 Hz) so you retain body. Use a narrow cut at 300–500 Hz if the kit sounds muddy.
  
  For transient shaping, put a transient shaper on the close conga with attack increased slightly and sustain reduced to taste (attack around +10–20%, sustain around -10–25% depending on the material), which brings the initial slap forward without making it brittle. On the buss, run a glue compressor with a medium attack and release and 2–4 dB gain reduction to sit everything together. Parallel compression works wonders: send the congas to a parallel buss, smash with heavy compression (50–80 ms attack, fast release) and blend back 10–30% to retain dynamics while adding punch.
  
  EQ to carve space: boost 3–6 kHz for presence on the attack, but if the vocal lives there, dip the highest percussion around 2–3 kHz to avoid masking. Use subtle saturation or tape emulation on the perc buss to add harmonic glue (drive low, 1–3 dB). For stereo placement, pan small percussion wider and keep the groove anchors slightly off-center so the overall pocket remains focused. Reverb should be short and dark on percussion (pre-delay 10–20 ms, decay 300–450 ms) so you get space without washing transients.
  
  Practice this: grab a multitrack percussion session, create busses, apply the transient shaping and parallel compression described, and render an A/B comparison. Listen for how the snappy hits change and write one note about what you fixed. Tip: practice this for 20 minutes each day and your ear will learn the pocket fast. Métele confianza, bro — ese ajuste pequeño cambia todo.

task_instruction: Coach on vocal comping and preserving emotional take while cleaning edits.
task_details: Provide a mentoring lesson on comping multiple vocal takes for a bilingual singer, how to make editing decisions that preserve phrasing and emotional nuances, basic tuning approach, and give a simple exercise to comp a verse and a chorus from provided takes.
personalized:
Hey — vocals are the heart, so we comp for story and feel, not just pitch. Start by listening to all takes once without marking anything; hear which phrases have the emotion you want. Create a master comp playlist and pick the best emotional phrase from each take rather than hunting for a perfect waveform. When you splice, make crossfades short (5–15 ms) and align breaths so phrasing breathes naturally. For bilingual singers, pay attention to Spanish syllable stress and consonant timing — a slight lead or lag can change the delivery entirely, so trust your ear.
  
  For tuning, do minimal corrective moves first: pitch drift and obvious outliers get a pass with your preferred tool, but keep vibrato and small pitch slides that are part of the performance. Use formant preservation if you need to shift large amounts so timbre stays natural. Automation is your friend: ride the gain rather than over-compressing, and clip gain small edits to keep breath dynamics.
  
  Practical exercise: comp the verse and chorus from four takes, preserve the one take's unique ad-libs if they add character, and deliver a clean comp with a short note explaining why you chose each phrase. Include timestamps for two micro-edits you made (e.g., vocal cut at 0:32.450 to remove a click). Tip: practica esto cada día for a week and focus on maintaining phrasing more than perfect pitch. You're building taste, not just a technical skill — la verdad, that nuance is what labels hear first.

task_instruction: Write a session call sheet and instructions for a live percussion tracking day.
task_details: Create a concise session plan for tracking a percussionist in-studio: show time, equipment list, mic placements, signal chain, monitoring setup, click vs. feel guidance, warm-up routine, and a short checklist for the engineer and the musician. Keep instructions clear and directive.
personalized:
Morning, team — here's the plan for percussion tracking tomorrow so we run smooth and focused. Call time 10:00 AM, soundcheck 10:15, warm-up and vibe talk at 10:30, tracking block from 11:00–2:00 with a 30-minute lunch break. Bring a matched pair small diaphragm condensers, a dynamic for close conga, a ribbon for room if you have one, DI for any shaker with pickup, and extra cables. Patch list: preamps on channels 1–8, 48V phantom on condensers, high-pass filters available on mic pre.
  
  Mic placements: conga dynamic 5–10 cm from the head at a 45-degree angle, overheads in ORTF around 60–80 cm to capture ensemble, room pair 2–3 m back. Signal chain: preamp → LA2A-style compressor on insert (track lightly), gain staging so peaks stay around -12 dBFS, and record to separate tracks for each mic. Monitoring: engineer sends an in-ear or foldback mix with the click at -12 dB plus a dry fold of the room to keep feel. Decide before the take if we use click: if the arrangement needs strict alignment with electronic elements, use a soft click on 2/4; if the take is standalone for sampling, we track without click and document BPM later.
  
  Warm-up: five minutes of scales and the groove phrase we'll record, then two full takes to test levels. Checklist for engineer and musician: check phase between mics, confirm preamp gain, record 30 seconds of room tone, label takes clearly (date_instrument_take), and save backups to external immediately after the block. Quick tip to the musician: play its natural groove first, then add accents on the second pass — we'll comp. Keep instructions tight and decisive in the room; that keeps the vibe and the edits easy. Vamos con todo.

task_instruction: Provide career advice on pitching to labels and building an A&R-friendly portfolio.
task_details: Offer mentorship on how to assemble a producer portfolio for pitching to labels and music supervisors: what to include (stems, finished tracks, reference tracks, credits), how to write a short outreach email, how to follow up, and a weekly practice habit to build network and craft.
personalized:
Parcero, here's how you make your work easy to listen to and hard to ignore. Your portfolio should have three polished finished tracks that show range, plus two stem packs geared for sync use (instrumental, full mix, and acapella). Include a one-page PDF with credits, roles for each track, and a short bio in English and Spanish highlighting your ethnographic sources and production specialties. Add a link to a private SoundCloud playlist and a Dropbox with stems (labeled and zipped).
  
  Outreach should be short and confident: introduce yourself in one line, link to the most relevant track, and propose a clear next step (listen to X for a sync idea or would you like stems for a quick demo). Subject lines matter: keep them specific and useful (producer_portfolio_artist_genre). Follow-up once after seven days with a friendly reminder and a fresh listening suggestion, and stop spam — quality over quantity. For conferences, have two concise stories: one about a project and one about a rhythm you researched — those are conversational hooks.
  
  Weekly habits: spend two hours improving one track and two hours contacting three targeted people with a personal note — not a template. Practice giving a 30‑second elevator pitch of your sound and another 30 seconds about why you work with field recordings. Tip: keep a spreadsheet of who you contacted, what they replied, and the next action. Métele un poco de paciencia and show consistent value, and portas las puertas se abren.

task_instruction: Advise on preparing a DJ set for an intimate Latin fusion night.
task_details: Walk an intern through planning a 45-minute DJ set that blends vinyl crate finds and original productions, covering track selection, BPM mapping, harmonic mixing tips, use of stems and acapellas for live mashups, and how to read and adapt to a small crowd. Include a practice routine to refine transitions and a short tech checklist for the venue.
personalized:
Alright DJ prep for an intimate spot: start by picking a mood arc — build from mellow cumbia and son jarocho remixes into higher-energy disco-cumbia hybrids, peaking about 30 minutes in and cooling down for the close. Map your set BPMs early and plan two or three anchor tracks where you'll mix between tempos (use tempo slows or harmonic mixing to morph smoothly). Keep your vinyl warm for color and have digital stems for vocal throws or drops when you want to create a live hybrid.
  
  For harmonic mixing, group tracks by key or compatible modes so your blends keep musical sense. Use short loops of a vocal acapella over a deep percussion loop to create bridges and try a simple beat-juggle to lift the chorus. When playing vinyl to digital transitions, use a clean filter sweep and a quick delay send to mask timing differences. Read the room: if people are dancing more to low-end, stay in that pocket; if they respond to melody, bring in a familiar vocal or refrain.
  
  Practice routine: rehearse the full 45 minutes twice, focusing on three transitions that need tightening, and record both rehearsals to critique timing and energy flow. Tech checklist for the venue: bring backup needles, an interface, stems on USB and in the cloud, and a small mixer with spare cables. Tip: arrive early for a soundcheck, and have a quiet two-track preview of your set for the promoter. Si te metes con ganas, la gente siente la intención.

task_instruction: Outline best practices for organizing a sample library and field notes.
task_details: Explain an organizational system for samples and field-recording notes: folder structure, naming conventions, metadata tagging, backup strategy, and a daily habit to maintain the library. Include instructions for tagging rhythmic, tonal, location, and legal/clearance flags.
personalized:
Bro, the value of your sample library is in how findable it is. Use a consistent folder hierarchy: Samples/Field/YYYY_MM_Location/Instrument_TakeNumber. File names should be explicit: 2025_03_Popayan_conga_take01_48k_24b.wav. Add a text file in each location folder with context — who you recorded, permissions, and short ethnographic notes (this is crucial for clearance and ethical use).
  
  Tagging matters: create a simple metadata sheet or use a DAW tagger and label items with rhythm type (cumbia, tumbao), feel (laid-back, aggressive), tempo range, key if tonal, and a clearance flag (cleared, needs permission, personal-use-only). Backups should be twofold: one local NAS and one cloud (encrypted if you prefer), and do monthly checksum verification. Keep a running spreadsheet index so you can filter by city, instrument, or tempo within seconds.
  
  Daily habit: spend 15 minutes after a session to import, name, tag, and write the short note while memory is fresh. That small routine avoids a decade of messy files. Tip: keep your best one-shots in a 'Top Hits' folder for quick access during sessions. Practica esto cada día and your crate-digging will be faster and more respectful to the people who shared their music with you.

The reverb tail in the bridge is a touch long (cut decay by 100–150 ms) so the words remain intelligible.

task_instruction: Write a concise project summary that presents the overall objectives and significance.
task_details: Compose a formal project summary for a grant panel that describes a two-year fieldwork initiative to document and archive traditional percussion-based musical practices in rural Andean and Pacific coastal communities, emphasizing objectives, significance for cultural preservation and contemporary music production, and primary deliverables (archival audio, metadata, and public-facing workshops). Use polished long sentences, minimal colloquial language, and include technical recording fidelity targets and expected audience impact.
personalized:
Dear Members of the Panel,

This proposal seeks funding for a two-year fieldwork initiative that documents and archives percussion-based musical practices across selected rural communities in the Andean highlands and Pacific coastal regions, with the dual objectives of preserving endangered sonic traditions and translating identified rhythmic vocabularies into pedagogical materials and contemporary production tools for emerging Latin music artists. The project prioritizes high-resolution audio capture (96 kHz, 24-bit) using industry-standard probes and microphones (Zoom H6 and Neumann KM184 pair for ambient stereo; Sennheiser MKH 416 for close vocal percussion), systematic metadata collection compliant with international archival standards, and culturally sensitive collaboration modalities that ensure community consent, compensation, and shared ownership of outputs. Deliverables will include a curated archival collection of raw and edited stems with contextual metadata, a public-facing series of workshops in each participating community to reinvest knowledge locally and to develop bilingual guides for producers and educators, and an online repository for researchers and practitioners that balances open-access dissemination with community-defined restrictions. The proposed work is significant because it offers a praxis-oriented model that connects ethnographic fieldwork with the pragmatic needs of contemporary music production and education, thereby preserving sonic heritage while generating economically and creatively sustainable pathways for communities and artists alike.

Sincerely,
Mateo Álvarez

personalized:
Dear Review Committee,

The methodology for this fieldwork is designed to produce archive-quality materials while ensuring replicable, ethically grounded practice; site selection will follow stratified purposive criteria that emphasize geographic diversity (Andean highland villages, Pacific coastal hamlets), vitality indicators of musical practice (frequency of communal events, number of active practitioners), and existing local partnerships that facilitate logistical and cultural mediation. Participant sampling will combine snowball referral with targeted invitations to recognized tradition-bearers, percussion ensembles, and younger practitioners engaged in hybrid production work, thereby capturing both intergenerational transmission and contemporary adaptation. Recording configurations will be standardized across sites to permit comparative analysis: primary stereo ambient capture using a matched pair of Neumann KM184 microphones on a stereo bar, close microphones for percussion and voice using Sennheiser MKH 416 and Shure SM57 where appropriate, and a Sound Devices MixPre-6 (or equivalent) preamp and recorder for low-noise capture (96 kHz, 24-bit WAV), with backup recordings to a secondary Zoom H6 unit (48 kHz) to mitigate data loss. All recordings will adhere to a documented signal chain and gain structure (no compression in the field; conservative headroom of 12 dB), and metadata will be captured contemporaneously using a field log protocol developed for this project that records participant names, instrument identification (instrument family and local term, e.g., ‘‘bata,’’ ‘‘tumbadora’’), GPS coordinates, event context, and recorded sample rates and bit depths. Postproduction will employ Pro Tools for assembly and light restorative editing, along with iZotope RX for noise reduction where necessary, while final archival masters will be exported as uncompressed WAV files (96 kHz, 24-bit) with embedded XML metadata and mirrored in compressed FLAC for repository access. This methodological approach therefore balances archival rigor, ethical sensitivity, and practical interoperability with contemporary production workflows used by label and sync partners.

task_instruction: Draft a narrative describing community engagement, reciprocity, and workshop plans.
task_details: Create a formal narrative for the grant panel that explains how the project will engage communities ethically, outline the content and structure of community workshops (aimed at both preservation and skill-building for young producers), detail compensation and benefit-sharing mechanisms, and describe measures to ensure the community retains agency over recordings. Use long, formal sentences and include expected local outcomes.
personalized:
Dear Members of the Panel,

Community engagement is central to the proposed fieldwork and is structured to ensure reciprocity, agency, and tangible benefits for participating communities; prior to any recording, the project will initiate a series of community meetings facilitated by bilingual cultural liaisons to explain objectives, rights, and potential uses of the recordings, and to obtain informed, recorded consent in both Spanish and local vernaculars where applicable. Workshops delivered in each community will combine three complementary modules: an archival literacy session that clarifies metadata and custodial procedures and demonstrates how materials will be stored and accessed; a technical skills module that introduces basic field-recording techniques and affordable approaches to documenting rhythm and song using mobile devices and portable recorders (Zoom H6 demonstrations and microphone placement exercises); and a creative production lab that pairs local percussionists with emerging producers to explore how traditional grooves can be arranged and legally sampled into contemporary tracks, thereby generating immediate economic opportunities. Compensation will include honoraria for participants, a shared revenue arrangement for any commercial exploitation of recorded material (documented in written agreements), and investment in local infrastructure such as donated storage drives and community-access playback devices. Furthermore, the project will establish a community advisory board with representatives from each site to review dissemination plans and to set access restrictions where cultural sensitivity requires localized control, thereby ensuring that custodial decisions remain grounded in community preferences and that benefits are equitably distributed.

task_instruction: Provide a data management and archiving plan describing formats, repositories, and access policies.
task_details: Write a formal data management plan for the grant panel that states file formats, backup strategies, metadata standards (e.g., Dublin Core), long-term repository selection, preservation workflows, and access protocols that balance open dissemination and community restrictions. Include transfer and storage logistics and planned partnerships with institutional archives.
personalized:
Dear Review Panel,

The data management and archiving plan for this project is designed to ensure the long-term preservation, discoverability, and ethically governed access of field-recorded materials; primary masters will be stored as uncompressed WAV files (96 kHz, 24-bit) with embedded descriptive metadata, and derivative files for public access will be generated in FLAC and high-quality MP3 formats to facilitate distribution without compromising archival integrity. Metadata will adhere to established schemas (Dublin Core for descriptive fields, PREMIS for preservation actions, and local community-defined descriptors for culturally specific terms), and each recording will be accompanied by a standardized XML sidecar containing contextual information, participant consent status, and rights statements. The preservation workflow will include immediate triple-backup of raw files on encrypted solid-state drives in the field, secure transfer (SFTP with checksums) to a central institutional server upon return, and subsequent mirroring to a partner university archive and a culturally appropriate national repository (negotiated memoranda of understanding with both institutions will outline custodial responsibilities). Access policies will be governed by a tiered model that respects community preferences: fully open access will be available for materials that communities identify as non-sensitive, whereas restricted access or permission-based review will apply to ritual or sacred recordings as determined by the community advisory board. Furthermore, the project will maintain a searchable online catalog that exposes metadata and non-sensitive audio excerpts for researchers and educators while providing an application mechanism for access to full masters, thereby balancing scholarly utility with cultural stewardship.

task_instruction: Write an ethics and consent protocol describing participant protections and intellectual property arrangements.
task_details: Compose a formal ethics narrative for a grant panel that details the informed consent process, bilingual consent forms, procedures for negotiating intellectual property and benefit-sharing, anonymization options for participants, and mechanisms for community oversight. Include how field payments or honoraria will be handled and recordkeeping for consent.
personalized:
Dear Committee Members,

Ethical conduct is foundational to this project and is operationalized through a comprehensive consent and intellectual property protocol that foregrounds participant autonomy and equitable benefit-sharing; informed consent will be obtained in writing and recorded verbally (Spanish and, where necessary, local languages), using clear bilingual forms that specify the intended uses of recordings, data retention periods, distribution channels, compensation arrangements, and options for revocation or anonymization. The project will offer choices to participants regarding the level of public exposure for their recordings, including full public release, restricted academic access, or archival preservation with community-controlled access, and these preferences will be documented in a consent registry that accompanies the metadata for each item. Intellectual property negotiations will be formalized via simple, culturally appropriate agreements that specify revenue-sharing percentages for any commercial licensing and that guarantee a share of proceeds to named tradition-bearers and to community development funds, thereby aligning commercial outcomes with local benefit. Honoraria will be disbursed transparently at the time of participation and will be recorded in financial logs, and additional provisions will be made for community events and materials (such as recorded copies, printed transcriptions, and donated equipment). Oversight will be provided by a community advisory board that reviews proposed uses of materials and has the authority to recommend additional protections or restrictions, thereby ensuring that ethical governance remains responsive to community values and expectations.

task_instruction: Outline a detailed timeline with milestones for the two-year project.
task_details: Provide a formal timeline narrative that specifies phases (preparation, fieldwork rounds, postproduction, workshops, archiving, dissemination), estimated month ranges for each activity, deliverables at each milestone, and contingency allowances. Present as prose with long, linked sentences rather than lists.
personalized:
Dear Panel,

The project timeline is organized into sequential and overlapping phases across a twenty-four month period, beginning with a three-month preparation phase that comprises partnership agreements, finalization of field protocols, procurement and testing of recording equipment (Zoom H6, Neumann KM184, Sennheiser MKH 416, MixPre-6), and the development of bilingual consent materials and metadata templates, and which will culminate in a preparatory workshop with community liaisons. Fieldwork will be conducted in two six-month rounds, the first concentrating on the Andean highland sites (months 4 through 9) and the second on Pacific coastal communities (months 10 through 15), with each round allocating time for intensive recording sessions, community meetings, and reciprocal workshops that return preliminary edits to participants for feedback. Months 16 through 20 will be devoted to postproduction and archival preparation, including audio restoration, metadata finalization, and the creation of pedagogical materials and producer toolkits; during this interval the project will also negotiate deposit procedures with partner archives. Months 21 and 22 will focus on dissemination activities such as a regional symposium, public exhibitions of the sonic materials, and the launch of an online catalog with tiered access, while months 23 and 24 will address evaluation, final reporting to funders, and the transfer of remaining archival copies to institutional partners. The timeline therefore integrates field documentation with iterative community review and dissemination, and includes contingency buffers to accommodate weather-related delays, participant availability constraints during seasonal events, and additional time for rights negotiations as they arise.

task_instruction: Compose a budget justification narrative explaining major cost categories and value for money.
task_details: Write a formal budget narrative for the grant panel that explains personnel costs (field engineers, cultural liaisons), equipment purchases and rentals, travel and lodging, participant compensation, postproduction and archiving costs, and indirect costs, highlighting cost-effectiveness and in-kind contributions. Use long, precise sentences and tie expenditures to project outcomes.
personalized:
Dear Review Committee,

The proposed budget allocates resources to line items that are directly tied to the quality and sustainability of the work, and personnel costs reflect the need for a small, specialized team composed of a lead field producer (project director), two field engineers with expertise in high-resolution capture and mic techniques, and bilingual cultural liaisons from partner communities who will coordinate logistics and ethical facilitation; these roles are essential to guarantee both technical excellence and culturally informed engagement. Equipment expenditures prioritize durable, archive-grade hardware (purchase of two matched Neumann KM184 microphones, one Sennheiser MKH 416, a Sound Devices MixPre-6, and three solid-state drives for redundant backing) and are justified by the long-term utility of these assets for follow-on projects and for donated support to community archives. Travel and lodging budgets are calculated to enable extended stays in rural sites to coincide with local musical events and to reduce repeated transport costs, and participant compensation is budgeted as honoraria for tradition-bearers and stipends for community workshop attendees to recognize time and knowledge contributions. Postproduction and archiving costs include technician time for audio restoration (Pro Tools and iZotope RX licenses), repository deposit fees, and the production of bilingual pedagogical materials and storage drives for community retention. Indirect costs cover institutional administration necessary for secure data handling and fiscal compliance, and in-kind contributions from partner institutions (archival storage space and exhibition venues) are documented to enhance value for money while minimizing duplicative spending.

task_instruction: Describe dissemination and impact plans for academic, industry, and community stakeholders.
task_details: Provide a formal dissemination narrative for a grant panel explaining how the project will share results with academic researchers, music industry partners, and participating communities, including workshops, symposia, open-access repositories, producer toolkits, and potential licensing pathways for commercial use. personalized:
Dear Panel Members,

Dissemination will be executed across three complementary streams to maximize scholarly, industry, and community impact: academic dissemination will include conference presentations and peer-reviewed articles that analyze rhythmic taxonomies and transmission modalities, leveraging the project's standardized metadata for reproducibility and cross-site comparison; industry-facing outputs will consist of curated stem packs and producer toolkits (arranged multitrack stems with tempo maps and licensing templates) that enable label partners and emerging producers to responsibly integrate traditional rhythms into contemporary productions while ensuring benefit-sharing. Community dissemination will prioritize immediate, accessible outcomes such as bilingual workshops that return edited recordings to participants, local listening sessions that document community consent for broader use, and donated playback drives and printed materials for educational programs. Impact will be measured by specific indicators including the number of archived recordings deposited with partner repositories, the count of community workshops delivered and participants trained, licensing agreements that include benefit-sharing clauses, and citations of the archive in scholarly works and creative productions; furthermore, long-term indicators will track whether community-managed access policies are enacted and whether participating youth demonstrate increased capacity in field recording and production skills, thereby evidencing both cultural preservation and local economic opportunity.

task_instruction: Write a capacity building and training plan for local collaborators and youth participants.
task_details: Create a formal narrative for the grant panel that outlines training modules, mentorship strategies, equipment handover plans, and evaluation methods to build local capacity in field recording, metadata management, and basic production. Include timelines for training, selection criteria for trainees, and how this supports sustainability.
personalized:
Dear Members of the Selection Committee,

The capacity building component of this project is structured to leave durable technical and archival skills within participating communities through a series of modular trainings and mentorship pairings that span the fieldwork and postproduction phases; trainee selection will favor local technicians, interested youth, and active musicians who demonstrate commitment to ongoing documentation, and selection will be conducted in consultation with community leaders to ensure inclusivity and local relevance. Training modules will include hands-on instruction in microphone selection and placement, field recording best practices (gain staging, redundancy, and metadata logging), basic postproduction techniques for editing and rendering stems in Pro Tools and Ableton, and metadata entry aligned with archival standards, with practical exercises culminating in participant-led documentation of a community event. Mentorship strategies will pair each trainee with a field engineer for on-the-job learning during the recording rounds and will include follow-up remote consultations during postproduction; additionally, the project will provide community-owned equipment packages (portable recorder, matched microphones, and a hardened external drive) upon successful completion of training, thereby facilitating ongoing documentation independent of external funding. Evaluation will employ pre- and post-training assessments of technical competencies, participant self-reports of confidence in equipment handling, and review of trainee-produced recordings against quality benchmarks, and these measures will inform iterative improvements to the curriculum and confirm that investments contribute to long-term sustainability.

personalized:

This proposal is supported by a consortium of institutional and community partners whose commitments are documented herein and which collectively strengthen the project's capacity for ethical documentation, archiving, and dissemination; the university archive partner has agreed to accept a copy of the full archival masters for long-term custodial preservation, to provide trained archival staff time for metadata ingestion and preservation planning, and to host a public symposium that presents preliminary findings. These partners will participate in a governance framework that convenes quarterly to review project progress, to adjudicate sensitive release requests from external researchers or industry partners, and to approve final deposit and licensing conditions, thereby ensuring that responsibilities for preservation, training, and public presentation are clearly allocated and operationalized through mutually accountable mechanisms.

task_details: Focus on Mateo's ethnomusicology curiosity, field recording practice, and crate-digging. Mention trips to small towns across Latin America, using portable mic setups, analog synths, and late-night phone notes. Include an anecdote of chasing a groove in an Oaxacan mercado. personalized: Mateo Álvarez moves like a cartographer of sound, notebook in one hand, a worn Zoom in the other, sketching rhythms in marketplaces and backrooms from Cali to Oaxaca. He listens first—breath of a singer, scrape of a wooden box, motor hum—then folds those textures into his studio mixes, layering congas and analog synths until a chorus blooms. Once, in a mercado in Oaxaca, he chased a tiny tumbao that people danced to between stalls; he recorded the vendor’s whistles, a passing lowrider, and built the hook around that human noise. His work reads like field notes set to pop craft: ethnomusicology curiosity tempered by a radio-ready sense of structure. He mentors young producers with the same patience he uses in the field—showing how to capture a moment and make it travel. The result is music that smells like tierra and gasoline, that lifts the chorus and keeps the groove in the pocket.

task_instruction: Direct a lead vocal tracking pass with comping and strict technical parameters.

task_instruction: Coordinate a full band live tracking pass for rhythm section.
task_details: Track drums, bass, rhythm guitar, and keys live to capture the 'in-the-room' feel. Use isolation where necessary. Click at 95 BPM. Provide track labels, mic lists for drums, bleed mitigation notes, count-ins, and instructions for stem exports. Include precise channel routing.

Session: RHYTHM_LIVE. Click: 95 BPM, set to all foldbacks at -10 dB.

Bass: DI (Track 9), Bass Mic/Amp (10). Guitar: DI + Amp mic (11/12). Keys: Stereo DI (13/14).
Bleed mitigation: gobos between amps and drum kit. Keep guitar amp stage left 2 m from drum kit. Use cloth dampers on cymbals if spill exceeds -18 dB.

task_instruction: Set up and track an acoustic drum kit for a Latin groove with phase and tuning checks.
task_details: Mic the kit for a tight, room-aware Latin groove (kick, snare, hats, congas integration). Provide mic list, placements, phase check steps, drum tuning notes, compression settings for snare buss, and count-in. Label track channels clearly and include post-session editing guidelines.
personalized:
Drum tracks: KICK_IN (2), KICK_OUT (3), SN_TOP (4), SN_BOT (5), HIHAT (6), TOM1 (7), TOM2 (8), OH_L/R (9/10), ROOM_L/R (11/12).
Kick mic: AKG D112 inside beater (3 cm), OUT: Beta52 (1 m front). Snare top: SM57 (2 cm), bottom: small-diaphragm (phase inverted). Hi-hat: small-diaphragm 10 cm above edge. OH: Neumann KM184 pair (spaced), Room: Royer R-121 ribbon at 3 m.
Phase check: solo kick IN+OUT, flip polarity if any cancellation under 120 Hz. Check snare top/bot for 180° alignment. Tune toms to match cumbia timbre (toms tuned mid-high). Dampen cymbal ring if spilling into mic too much.
Set snare buss compression: 4:1, 6 ms attack, 100 ms release, make-up +2 dB (apply in mix, not on record). Click: 95 BPM, drummer to lead. Count-in: ready in 4 — 3 — 2 — 1 — play.
Record two takes. Label with TAKE markers and note any stick changes. Post-session: supply unprocessed multitracks and an edited kit stem with bleed reduction markers. [EXPORT: DRUMS_RAW_24-48, KIT_EDIT]

task_instruction: Create two headphone monitor mixes for the vocalist and drummer with exact send levels.
task_details: Produce headphone mix A for vocalist (more dry lead, light reverb) and mix B for drummer (click louder, bass clearer). Specify aux sends, reverb levels, click dB relative to lead, and label headphone amp outputs. Include immediate change procedure and countdown for live session adjustments.
personalized:
Headphone Mix A: VOC_MON (Head Amp 1). Lead vocal +0 dB, instrumental -6 dB, click -8 dB, reverb send 12% (aux 2). Pan instruments centered. Headphone output H1.
Headphone Mix B: DRUM_MON (Head Amp 2). Click +2 dB relative to lead, bass +1.5 dB, guitar -3 dB, vocal -6 dB. Reverb send 6% only on snare. Headphone output H2.

Ready to cue in 1 minute. Count-in for tracking: ready in 3 — 2 — 1. Post-session: save two cue mix snapshots as HEADPHONE_A.snapshot and HEADPHONE_B.snapshot. [SAVE: HEADPHONE_A, HEADPHONE_B]

persona.profession: Music Producer / A&R Producer specializing in Latin rhythms and pop fusion
persona.education: B.M. in Music Production and Engineering, Berklee College of Music; Pro Tools and Ableton Certified; short courses in ethnomusicology and field recording
persona.socioeconomic_status: Upper-Middle Income; freelance producer with steady label and sync clients
persona.brief_background: He builds tracks by layering live percussion and field recordings gathered on trips to small towns across Latin America, then shapes them into radio-friendly pop arrangements. Mateo splits his time between studio sessions with emerging artists and consulting for label A&R teams, often translating traditional rhythms into hooks that can move international audiences. He keeps long lists of sample sources and phone notes from late-night conversations with folkloric musicians — and will drop everything to chase a new groove he heard on a trip.
persona.interests_lifestyle: crate-digging vinyl, hand percussion (congas, cajón, bata), salsa and cumbia nights, field recording on location, vintage synths and analog gear, bilingual songwriting and lyric coaching, DJ sets at intimate venues, mentoring young producers, traveling Latin America for musical research, experimenting with fusion arrangements

general_writing_style.tone: Warm, collaborative and slightly playful, but always expert and goal-oriented — he balances enthusiasm for new grooves with clear expectations about deadlines and deliverables. He uses encouraging language when mentoring or developing artists, and a more decisive, no-fluff register when directing studio sessions or giving notes.
general_writing_style.syntax: Mixes short, imperative sentences for session direction and quick requests with longer, compound-complex sentences when describing arrangement choices or musical context. Prefers active voice and present tense, often inserting parenthetical technical asides (e.g., "low-cut at 120 Hz") and timestamped notes to be actioned.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Combines studio/production jargon ("stems," "buss," "aux send," "glue compressor," "transient shaping," "BPM," "dB," "Hz") with ethnomusicology and Latin-rhythm terms ("cumbia," "bata," "tumbao," "son jarocho"). He freely code-switches for warmth or emphasis, using Colombian colloquialisms like "parcero," "qué nota" or "chévere," alongside technical requests such as "send me the stems," "high-pass the room mics," or "let's lock the groove at 95 BPM."
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent code-switching between English for technical detail and Spanish for color or encouragement; regular contractions like "I'm," "we'll," "let's." He uses musical metaphors and short performance-focused phrases repeatedly, e.g. "in the pocket," "lift the chorus," "that take has vibe," and conversational tags such as "la verdad" or "bro" — examples: "Send me the stems," "esa conga está en el pocket," "let's lock it in," "qué nota, parcero."

contextual_writing_style.scenario_description: To a young niece or nephew in the form of a short bedtime story inspired by rhythms and travel.
contextual_writing_style.detailed_style: Playful, lyrical, and sensory with short simple sentences, repetitive rhythmic phrasing, and affectionate Spanish diminutives; prioritize imagery and sound words to make the story musical when read aloud. Use gentle repetition and onomatopoeia to mimic percussion and create a soothing cadence.
contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Simple sentence structures, repeated refrains, and onomatopoetic words that imitate instruments; affectionate Spanish terms peppered throughout. Example phrases: "El pequeño tambor decía pum-pum", "la brisa olía a caña y café", "duerme, mi niño, sueña con la pista". Scenario-specific features: rhythmic punctuation to simulate beats, repeated hooks like "pum-pum" or "ta-ta-ta," and diminutives such as "pequeñito" to soften tone.

task_instruction: Tell a jungle rhythm bedtime story using bata drums and animal characters.
task_details: Create a short bedtime tale (6–10 short sentences) set in a jungle where bata drums call the animals. Include onomatopoeia like "boom-boom" and repeated refrains. Give each animal a tiny affectionate nickname (e.g., "monito"). Use sensory imagery (damp earth, sweet fruit) and finish with a calming line for sleep.
personalized: En la selva la lluvia canta. El bata dice boom-boom. El monito aplaude clac-clac. La tortuguita marca un paso lento. Boom-boom, boom-boom, todos siguen el pulso. La tierra huele a tierra mojada y a guayaba. Duerme, mi pequeñito, con los tambores en calma. Boom-boom, dulce sueño, mi amor.

task_instruction: Write a rhythm-of-the-rail bedtime story for a young child.
task_details: Produce a short bedtime story (5–8 short sentences) that mimics a gentle train ride through towns. Use repetitive onomatopoeia like "chucu-chucu" and include counting of stops (uno, dos, tres) as soothing repetition. Add affectionate Spanish diminutives and end with a lullaby-like refrain.
personalized: Vamos en tren, mi pequeñito. Las ruedas dicen chucu-chucu. Una estación, uno. Otra estación, dos. Chucu-chucu, chucu-chucu, la noche corre suave. El paisaje huele a papaya y a humo de cocina. Duerme, mi niño, sueña con estaciones. Chucu-chucu, buenas noches, mi amorcito.

task_instruction: Create a studio-themed bedtime story referencing field recordings and found sounds.
task_details: Write a short story (6–9 short sentences) written as if told by a producer to a niece/nephew about a tiny studio where field recordings come alive. Use simple sentences, gentle onomatopoeia for samples (e.g., "plop-plop," "tik-tik"), affectionate diminutives, and a refrain like "duerme, sueña con la pista." Keep technical jargon minimal and playful.
personalized: En mi estudio vive un grabador pequeño. Sus botoncitos hacen plop-plop. Un acento de lluvia dice tik-tik. Las grabaciones se vuelven cuentos. Plop-plop, tik-tik, la pista duerme. La brisa trae aromas de pueblo y tambores. Duerme, mi pequeñito, sueña con la pista. Plop-plop, dulces sueños, mi amor.

task_instruction: Write a street-market night lullaby featuring maracas and vendors.
task_details: Compose a short bedtime tale (6–8 short sentences) set in a night market where maracas and street musicians play. Use onomatopoeia like "chi-chi" and "pum-pum," include sensory smells (spices, roasting), affectionate diminutives, and a comforting refrain to close.

task_instruction: Compose a starry synth lullaby using vintage synth imagery.
task_details: Write a soothing bedtime story (5–7 short sentences) where vintage synths turn into stars. Use gentle onomatopoeia like "plink-plonk" and sensory phrases about cool night air. Include affectionate diminutives and a repeated refrain that sounds like a lullaby.
personalized: Las estrellas suenan como sintetizadores viejitos. Plink-plonk, plink-plonk, la galaxia parpadea. El aire nocturno huele a fruta y a sueño. Cada nota es una lucecita. Plink-plonk, plink-plonk, la noche mece la canción. Duerme, mi amorcito, sueña con pistas de estrellas. Plink-plonk, buenas noches, pequeñito.

task_instruction: Tell a story about an animal band traveling through Latin America.
task_details: Create a short bedtime story (7–10 short sentences) where different animals form a traveling band that plays rhythms from places Mateo visited. Assign an instrument to each animal (conga, cajón, maracas, guitar), use repeated refrains and onomatopoeia, include Spanish diminutives, and end with a gentle goodnight.
personalized: Había una banda de animalitos viajeros. La iguana toca la conga: pum-pum. La gallinita sacude maracas: chi-chi. El perrito toca cajón: ta-ta. El pajarito canta la melodía. Pum-pum, chi-chi, ta-ta, la ruta los abraza. Huelen a tierra y a frutas de viaje. Duerme, mi pequeñito, sueña con la banda. Pum-pum, dulces sueños, mi amor.
